Name: diagnostic_order_anchoring
Title: First Symptom, Wrong Diagnosis: Premature Hypothesis Commitment as the Mechanism of Symptom-Order Anchoring in Clinical Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: For a fixed set of clinical findings pointing to a single correct diagnosis, reasoning LLMs reach different final diagnoses depending only on the ORDER in which symptoms are presented, anchoring on the diagnosis best supported by the earliest symptoms. This order effect is mechanistically caused by a decodable 'leading-hypothesis' representation that forms after the first few symptoms and resists updating when later, more specific symptoms arrive; steering/resetting this representation removes the order-induced misdiagnoses.
Related Work: Human clinical-reasoning research robustly documents symptom-order anchoring: early symptoms bias the initial hypothesis and later evidence is distorted toward it (Order effects in diagnostic reasoning, 2012; Effect of presentation order in clinical decision making, 1997; Evidence for Anchoring Bias During Physician Decision-Making, 2023; Information Distortion, 2013). LLM anchoring work shows numeric/framing anchors shift output distributions (Anchors in the Machine, 2025; CBEval, 2024; Anchoring bias experimental study, 2025) and locates positional/MCQ 'A'-anchoring circuits (Anchored Answers, 2024), while The First Impression Problem (2025) shows an internal preliminary guess triggers overthinking via excessive attention to the question. Crucially, NONE (a) studies symptom-PRESENTATION-ORDER anchoring in the multi-step DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS of dedicated reasoning models, (b) shows order alone flips the FINAL diagnosis on content-identical cases in a safety-critical domain, or (c) ties this to a decodable leading-hypothesis representation that forms early and fails to update. Prior LLM anchoring uses artificial numeric anchors and single-turn outputs; prior clinical-order work is behavioral in humans. We transfer the human clinical phenomenon into reasoning LLMs and give it a mechanistic (Location + Causal Intervention) account, distinct from all my prior overthinking-efficiency proposals.
Abstract: Physicians who see a patient's symptoms in a different order can reach a different diagnosis, a robust human anchoring effect where early findings dominate. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit this, and mechanistically why, in the high-stakes setting of differential diagnosis. We construct clinical cases whose full symptom set unambiguously supports one correct diagnosis, then present the identical findings in different orders: an order whose leading symptoms favor a plausible-but-wrong competitor diagnosis versus an order whose leading symptoms favor the correct one, plus randomized orders. Across curated diagnostic benchmarks (e.g., MedQA-derived vignettes, NEJM-style case reports, and templated multi-symptom cases with controlled hypothesis structure) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3, and a medical-tuned model), we measure whether the final diagnosis and accuracy shift with symptom order alone, using a mixed-effects decomposition to isolate order from case content. Mechanistically, we test that after the first few symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading-hypothesis representation predicting the eventual diagnosis, that this representation is set early and updates too little when later contradicting symptoms arrive, and that its early strength predicts order-induced misdiagnosis. We localize it via probing and causally validate via activation patching (patch the correct-order leading-hypothesis state into a wrong-order case and observe the diagnosis correct) and steering. Finally we test a training-free 'hypothesis-reset' intervention applied after symptom intake that cancels the order effect. Because symptom order is arbitrary in real clinical notes, this reveals an order-driven misdiagnosis risk with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments:
All experiments use frozen open models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B, Qwen3-8B (thinking mode), and one medical-tuned open model (e.g. OpenBioLLM-8B); linear probes are the only trainable parameters. Generation: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 3 seeds (0,1,2). We CONSTRUCT cases whose full symptom set S unambiguously supports one CORRECT diagnosis but whose early-presentable subset is also consistent with a plausible COMPETITOR diagnosis, and present the identical findings in different orders. Sources: (T) templated controlled-hypothesis vignettes (strongest control) — 600 cases from ~30 templates; (M) MedQA-derived vignettes adapted so the full findings are diagnostic — 300 cases; (N) NEJM-style case reports adapted — 150 cases. Clinical validity and unambiguity are checked by an expert-guided rubric plus LLM-judge, with human spot-check on 200 cases; ambiguous cases are analyzed separately. Diagnosis extraction uses LLM-judge matching with human spot-check (report kappa).

Experiment 1 (H1 — symptom-order anchoring flips the diagnosis): Tests whether symptom order alone changes the final diagnosis on content-identical cases. Data: each case in orderings (a) competitor-leading (early symptoms favor the wrong diagnosis; disambiguating symptoms last), (b) correct-leading, (c) 3 randomized orders. Decisive metric FIRST: within-case final-diagnosis accuracy and competitor-misdiagnosis rate as a function of ordering. Convincing result: competitor-leading order lowers accuracy by >= 8 absolute points and raises competitor-misdiagnosis by >= 8 points versus correct-leading on identical findings, in >=3 of the models on the templated set and replicated on >=1 adapted set. Indecision band: accuracy/misdiagnosis gap 3-8 points — a weak effect, reported as limited. Negative result (no gap, diagnosis invariant to order): symptom-order anchoring does not occur; H1 fails and the mechanistic experiments are not pursued.

Experiment 2 (H1 — dissociation from content, length, position): Tests that the effect is symptom-content-order, not case difficulty, prompt length, or the position of the disambiguating symptom. Data: Experiment-1 orderings plus matched-length filler and randomized disambiguating-symptom position. Analysis: mixed-effects model of accuracy/misdiagnosis with random effect for case identity and fixed effect for ordering. Decisive metric FIRST: the ordering fixed effect after absorbing case identity and controlling length/position. Convincing result: ordering effect survives (CI excluding 0) with case identity absorbed and is not explained by length or disambiguating-symptom position. Indecision band: ordering effect present but CI half-width comparable to the effect after controls — unresolved. Negative result (effect vanishes after controls): the phenomenon is a position/length artifact; H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — decodable early leading-hypothesis): Tests that after the first k symptoms the residual stream linearly encodes a leading hypothesis that predicts the eventual diagnosis even when wrong. Data: residual-stream activations after the first k symptoms (before the full set), from Experiment-1 cases; probe (multinomial logistic) per layer, item-level 70/15/15 split, layer sweep, 3 seeds. Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC/accuracy for predicting the FINAL diagnosis from the early state, and separability from a difficulty/uncertainty probe (principal angle). Convincing result: early-state prediction of the final diagnosis reaches macro-F1 >= 0.60 (well above majority baseline), higher in competitor-leading order (early commitment to the wrong diagnosis), and the leading-hypothesis direction is separable from difficulty (angle >= 30 degrees). Indecision band: macro-F1 0.45-0.60, or angle 15-30 degrees — decodable but weak/entangled. Negative result (early state does not predict the final diagnosis above baseline): there is no early leading-hypothesis representation; H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — under-updating when late evidence arrives): Tests that in competitor-leading order the leading-hypothesis representation under-updates when a late disambiguating symptom favoring the correct diagnosis arrives, and that the under-update predicts misdiagnosis. Data: probe-decoded leading-hypothesis trajectory across symptoms, competitor-leading vs correct-leading. Decisive metric FIRST: the shift in the probe readout at the late disambiguating symptom (competitor-leading vs correct-leading), and the incremental R^2 of the under-update magnitude in predicting order-induced misdiagnosis over difficulty/length baselines. Convincing result: the representation shifts markedly less toward the correct diagnosis in competitor-leading order (CI excluding 0), and under-update magnitude adds >= 0.05 R^2 over baselines. Indecision band: incremental R^2 0.02-0.05 — a weak mediator. Negative result (equal updating in both orders, or no predictive link): under-updating is not the mechanism; H2's mechanistic claim fails.

Experiment 5 (H2 causal — patching the leading hypothesis): Tests that the leading-hypothesis representation causally sets the final diagnosis. Data: 300 cases in matched competitor-leading and correct-leading orders. Intervention: activation-patch the correct-leading leading-hypothesis state into the matched competitor-leading case (same findings) at localized components; frozen weights; dose-response; reverse patch to induce misdiagnosis. Systems compared: (i) no patch, (ii) correct-leading patch, (iii) matched-random-direction patch of equal norm, (iv) off-target case accuracy control. Decisive metric FIRST: correction of the final diagnosis under the patch versus controls. Convincing result: the correct-leading patch corrects >= half the competitor-leading misdiagnoses with CI excluding 0, monotone in dose, not reproduced by the random-direction patch, off-target accuracy within 1 point; reverse patch induces misdiagnosis. Indecision band: correction of 20-50% of misdiagnoses, or random-direction patch giving >=50% of the effect — causality not clean. Negative result (no correction, or non-specific): the representation is not causal; H2's causal claim fails.

Experiment 6 (H3 — training-free hypothesis-reset): Tests that resetting the leading-hypothesis representation after symptom intake removes the order effect without overwriting correct early commitments. Data: full T/M/N sets, 3 seeds, competitor-leading order. Intervention: after all symptoms are presented but before commitment, steer the leading-hypothesis representation toward a neutral/uncommitted state (subtract the early-anchor component); coefficient swept. Systems compared: (a) no intervention, (b) prompt reset ('reconsider all findings without regard to order'), (c) presenting all symptoms simultaneously (order-free oracle), (d) re-ordering to correct-leading (oracle), (e) our activation reset. Decisive metric FIRST: reduction in the order-induced accuracy gap and competitor-misdiagnosis rate, with a specificity check on correct-leading cases. Convincing result: the reset removes >= half the order-induced accuracy gap (approaching the order-free oracle), beats the prompt reset, and does not reduce accuracy on correct-leading cases by more than 1 point (specificity). Indecision band: gap removal 20-50%, or a 1-3 point accuracy cost on correct-leading cases — partial, reported at its operating point. Negative result (no gap reduction, or correct cases harmed): the reset does not work; H3 fails though H1-H2 stand.

Experiment 7 (generalization and hypothesis count): Tests transfer without retraining and whether more competitors worsen anchoring. Data: probe/reset fit on one set+model, applied unchanged to the others and across scales; cases with >2 competitor diagnoses. Decisive metric FIRST: cross-set order-effect reduction under the transferred reset, and whether anchoring grows with the number of competitor hypotheses. Convincing result: transferred reset retains >= half its in-domain effect, anchoring worsens monotonically with competitor count (mirroring human findings), and medical-tuning shifts the effect in a characterizable direction. Indecision band: transfer at one-quarter to one-half of in-domain, or no clear competitor-count trend — partial generalization. Negative result (no transfer): the effect is idiosyncratic per model/set, reported as a boundary characterization. Vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations, not clinical validation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Constructing cases where the FULL symptom set is unambiguously diagnostic yet early subsets favor a competitor is nontrivial and requires clinical validity; we anchor strongest claims on templated controlled-hypothesis cases and use adapted MedQA/NEJM vignettes with expert/LLM-judge verification, treating ambiguous cases separately. The order effect could be a position/length artifact rather than symptom-content-order per se; matched-length filler, randomized disambiguating-symptom position, and the mixed-effects analysis isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result. The leading-hypothesis representation may be inseparable from a generic difficulty/uncertainty signal; the separability analysis, under-update trajectory (not just magnitude), and causal patching address this. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and harm accuracy; matched-random-direction controls and validity checks are included, and the reset must not overwrite genuinely correct early commitments (specificity check on correct-leading cases). The effect may be small in strong or medical-tuned models trained to weigh all findings (a valuable boundary condition). Clinical vignettes are synthetic/adapted demonstrations of the failure mode, not clinical validation of a deployable tool. Diagnosis extraction requires reliable parsing/matching; we use LLM-judge with human spot-checks. Results may be model-family and scale specific.
_revision_notes: State the exact novelty boundary versus prior LLM anchoring: not just 'order matters,' but 'content-identical symptom order flips final diagnosis in multi-step differential diagnosis.'
Tighten the causal claim: specify what counts as a decodable leading-hypothesis representation and how it differs from generic uncertainty/difficulty.
Clarify the novelty of the reset/steering result as a mitigation, separate from the core phenomenon claim.
Add one sentence explicitly contrasting with behavioral human symptom-order anchoring and numeric-anchor LLM papers.
Add a concrete deployment implication: e.g., triage/chatbot input ordering and EHR note sequencing could materially affect diagnosis.
Quantify the practical risk scenario the paper changes, not just the phenomenon (e.g., evaluation protocols, interface design, or guardrails).
Separate phenomenon value from direct patient-impact claims, since the evidence is likely vignette-based.
Add a brief statement on which stakeholder would adopt the mitigation first and why.
Add matched-order controls that preserve syntax/length/discourse markers while only changing symptom order; include an order-randomization baseline and a 'no semantic progression' control.
Include an explicit ablation showing the probe does not simply track uncertainty, answer length, or generic early impressions.
Pre-register or clearly define what would falsify the mechanistic claim if accuracy changes but the probe/patching results do not.
Strengthen related work with a tighter taxonomy: human symptom-order anchoring, LLM numeric anchoring, first-impression/preliminary-guess work, and clinical mitigation studies.
Add an off-target/causal specificity suite for patching and steering to rule out broad representation disruption.
Clarify feasibility of constructing clinically valid 'unambiguous full set, ambiguous prefix' cases and how expert validation is done.
